payload.title: Something Old Something New Meaning and Origins
protect_keywords: something old something new something borrowed something blue
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, planning a wedding overseas, who want to know what the rhyme actually says, where it was first printed and what can honestly be said about each item, then choose pieces with real weight (a family heirloom, a commissioned new piece, something lent by a parent or grandparent, a blue detail that survives a long-haul flight) and get them to the destination safely.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the destination section.
payload.angle: Most pages repeat the rhyme, attach a neat meaning to each line and move on. We give the full wording with the sixpence line as Victorian periodicals printed it, dated by the scans themselves, and state a meaning only where a printed source gives one. Then we turn to how couples with real budgets do it now: an heirloom worn as is or reset, a piece commissioned for the day, something lent by family that goes back after the wedding, a blue detail chosen to travel well, and royal brides' lent and inherited pieces as the Royal Collection describes them. We finish with what no listicle covers: carrying irreplaceable pieces to a wedding overseas in hand luggage, with cover sorted before you fly.
must_include: About 10 numbered sections: the full rhyme and variants; earliest printed versions; something old; something new; something borrowed; something blue; the sixpence; royal and notable examples; modern and luxury ways to do each; carrying the items to a destination wedding
The rhyme quoted exactly as a dated printing gives it, including the sixpence line; earliest printing named by periodical and year, never 'first ever'
Meanings and origins stated as fact only where Opie and Tatem or a printed source gives them; otherwise confident living practice ('Many couples...'); 'often told' at most once
Royal and museum examples only as Royal Collection Trust and V&A pages describe them, cited once by link
Partners of any gender can carry the items; one line, said once
Destination section: heirlooms and jewellery in hand luggage, photograph and list pieces before travel, link to /style-advice/engagement-ring-insurance; no airline or insurance rules stated as fact
FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts (what does the rhyme mean, where does the sixpence go, who gives something borrowed, can the groom carry them, what counts as something blue)

Internal links: /expert-advice/wedding-traditions pillar; /style-advice/engagement-ring-insurance; /style-advice/lab-grown-diamonds; /style-advice/engagement-ring-styles; a destination hub where natural; /magazine; /wonderland-concierge

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, start no new reads after the limit, save after every 3 facts, never retry a declined call. Preferred sources: archive.org or HathiTrust scans of Victorian periodicals, Oxford Reference (Opie and Tatem, A Dictionary of Superstitions) if the entry shows, the Royal Mint (as a source, not a seller), the Royal Collection Trust, the V&A, Britannica. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs, phrases.org.uk or Wikipedia. Origins, dates and meanings are stated as fact only where a source gives them; everything else is written as living practice with no [[VERIFY]] marker; 'often told' at most once. Source gaps go in the run report only (authority rule).

facts_to_source: earliest printing found in a dated periodical scan, with title, volume, year and page

facts_to_source: the sixpence as a coin: first struck and withdrawn from circulation dates as the Royal Mint states them
the shoe line as printed in the rhyme sources
modern keepsake sixpences as living practice, no seller named

batch_A.section: Meaning of each item (old, new, borrowed, blue)

object number and date as the record gives them

batch_B.section: Modern and luxury ways to do each
